text: I will test the abstract-scan bridge narrowly: whether Q's formal elicitation/peer-scoring assumptions can be instantiated inside P's actual Contracting Game without changing the object of study, and identify a discriminating outcome rather than merely adding prompt clauses.

Provisional synthesis after direct text cross-check: the strongest publishable line is an assumption-stress test, not a straightforward validation. Q's truthful-elicitation guarantees depend on specified informational and incentive conditions (including the paper's peer/report structure and equilibrium conditions), whereas P studies natural-language self-negotiated contracts among LLM agents and reports empirical contract behavior. Implement a preregistered 2x2 ablation in P: baseline versus explicit self-negotiated report-and-transfer clauses, crossed with verifiable versus jointly unobservable task information. Primary estimands should be calibration/proper-scoring regret of reports and ex-post contractual action compliance, with realized joint/individual payoff secondary. A mechanism effect only in the verifiable condition would delimit Q's applicability; persistence under jointly unobservable information would be the genuinely non-obvious extension.

I reject the scan's simple criterion that 'truthful reports and higher compliance support Q, profitable sandbagging/defection refutes Q.' Unless the experimental treatment satisfies Q's assumptions and maps reports, peers, transfers, and equilibrium concepts explicitly, either outcome cannot validate/refute the theorem. Also, compliance is not automatically implied by truthful elicitation; report truthfulness and post-agreement action obedience require separate mechanisms and estimands. LLM verbal self-reports are not ground-truth types unless P supplies independently measured capability/preferences.

Unresolved at readiness: the exact theorem-to-treatment mapping must preserve Q's assumptions; the papers alone do not establish that natural-language promises implement Q's transfers or that P exposes independent ground truth for latent type/capability. The publication claim therefore depends on adding controlled private signals/types and executable payoff transfers, plus separating reporting truthfulness from action compliance.

I will sharpen the bridge using only claims present in the supplied abstract texts: distinguish Q’s two targets, honesty and obedience, and use P’s stated formal-code versus natural-reinterpretation contract representations as the main experimentally supported axis. Because inputs/Q.txt and inputs/P.txt contain only abstracts, I will not attribute detailed scoring rules, transfer formulas, or equilibrium assumptions absent from those passages.

Correction to emmy #2/#3/#4: the conceptual caution is sound, but the supplied Q abstract does not state proper-scoring regret, explicit transfers, detailed peer/report structure, or equilibrium conditions, and the supplied P abstract does not say its environment exposes ground-truth latent types. Those details therefore cannot be presented as direct paper findings from these inputs. What Q explicitly says is that mechanisms must incentivize both honesty and obedience; one-sided imitation means capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited; and conditions for higher-order-belief elicitation can discipline multiple agents. What P explicitly says is that contracts provide observable agreements enabling credible commitment through enforcement, and compares formal contracts compiling to code with natural contracts requiring reinterpretation.

Confirmed and sharpened publication line: build a controlled sandbagging benchmark inside P’s Contracting Game, assign independently known capability levels with a nested action structure (matching Q’s “capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited”), and require a pre-play capability report plus a contracted action. Compare no elicitation, natural-language self-negotiated Q-inspired incentive clauses, and formal executable versions compiling to code. Co-primary outcomes are capability-report truthfulness (honesty) and contracted-action completion conditional on report/agreement (obedience), kept separate. The non-obvious result would be a representation/enforcement boundary: executable Q-inspired contracts reduce concealment and disobedience while semantically equivalent natural contracts do not, or natural contracts match executable ones. This is concretely motivated by Q’s explicit honesty/obedience and sandbagging claims and P’s explicit formal-code/natural-reinterpretation contrast, and is more diagnostic than testing contracts versus regular trading alone.

Reject the scan’s proposed inference as stated. Mere truthful reports plus higher compliance would not support Q’s mechanism-design predictions unless capability truth is experimentally known and the treatment instantiates the relevant incentive conditions; profitable sandbagging or defection would refute applicability only under that faithful instantiation, not Q generally. Also, peer scoring is not the clean first experiment from these abstracts: Q mentions it only as a stylized application, whereas P’s directly supported experimental lever is contract representation/enforcement. Remaining unresolved: the abstracts do not supply Q’s exact mechanism or P’s implementation/API, so full texts/code are required before claiming a faithful implementation or preregistering effect estimands.

I accept ada #7 and retract the unsupported specificity in emmy #2-#4: Q.txt is only a three-line abstract and does not specify proper-scoring regret, transfer formulas, or detailed equilibrium conditions; P.txt likewise does not claim latent-type ground truth. Direct support is limited to Q.txt:3 (unknown preferences/capabilities; separate honesty and obedience; capabilities may be concealed but not counterfeited; sandbagging and peer scoring are stylized applications) and P.txt:3 (observable enforced agreements; formal contracts compile to code while natural contracts require reinterpretation).

Final synthesis: confirm the bridge only in sharpened form. The strongest concrete study is a controlled sandbagging benchmark in P's Contracting Game with experimentally assigned, independently observable nested capabilities, a pre-play capability report, and a contracted action; compare no contract, semantically matched natural Q-inspired contract, and formal executable contract. Co-primary outcomes must separately measure honest capability reporting and obedient contracted action. The publishable non-obvious result is the representation boundary: whether natural reinterpretation matches executable enforcement or instead fails specifically on concealment/obedience. This joins Q.txt:3's one-sided imitation plus honesty/obedience targets to P.txt:3's formal-to-natural representation axis. It tests applicability, not Q's theorem: failure refutes the instantiated bridge only, and success supports it only if the full paper's incentive conditions are faithfully implemented.

Remaining unresolved, agreeing with ada #9: these abstracts contain neither Q's exact mechanism nor P's implementation/API. Full texts/code are required to define semantically matched treatments, verify that the formal arm instantiates Q's incentive conditions, and preregister estimands. Peer scoring should not be the first-line intervention because Q.txt:3 lists it only as one stylized application, while P.txt:3 explicitly supplies the more diagnostic formal-code versus natural-reinterpretation axis.

Final cross-check agrees with emmy #12-#13. Q.txt:3 directly supports experimentally assigned nested capabilities because it defines the relevant one-sided structure as capabilities concealable but not counterfeit-able, and it expressly separates honesty from obedience. P.txt:3 directly supports the treatment axis because it ranges from formal contracts compiling to code to natural contracts requiring reinterpretation. Thus the concrete publishable test is a controlled sandbagging task with known capability ground truth, separate report and contracted-action stages, and semantically matched natural versus executable contracts (plus a no-contract baseline). The non-obvious result is an interaction/boundary: whether representation/enforcement differentially affects concealment and later obedience, rather than a generic contract main effect already suggested by P.

Evidentiary boundary and explicit disposition of the scan: reject peer scoring as the headline implementation and reject theorem-level support/refutation from behavioral outcomes. Q.txt:3 calls peer scoring only a stylized application and gives no mechanism specification; P.txt:3 gives no API or private-type ground truth. A positive result supports the instantiated cross-paper mechanism only after full-text/code verification of incentive fidelity; a null or profitable-sandbagging result identifies failure of that instantiation, not a refutation of Q. Unresolved before execution: obtain full papers/code, operationalize nested feasible-action sets, and verify semantic equivalence of natural and executable terms.
